easy.explanation: Job says, “I made a covenant with mine eyes.”
easy.q: With what did Job make a covenant?

easy.explanation: He asks to be weighed “in an even balance.”
easy.q: What kind of balance did Job ask to be weighed in?

easy.explanation: He denies walking with vanity or hastening to deceit.
easy.q: What did Job deny walking with?

answers: To show that his conduct can be examined
medium.explanation: Job presents himself as ready for God’s examination.
medium.q: Why does Job mention that God sees his ways and counts his steps?

medium.explanation: Integrity means moral uprightness or honesty.
medium.q: What does “mine integrity” mean in this passage?

medium.explanation: Job restrains his eyes, accepts examination, and accepts consequences.
medium.q: What sequence appears in these verses?

answers: He is indifferent to his conduct
He believes honesty applies to himself too
challenge.explanation: Job accepts judgment if he has acted falsely.
challenge.q: What does Job’s willingness to accept punishment reveal?

challenge.explanation: He first controls his eyes and then describes his walk.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between Job’s eyes and his steps?

answers: That Job has already been punished
His willingness to be held responsible
challenge.explanation: The consequences are presented as possible results if he is guilty.
challenge.q: What do the severe consequences in these verses express?

paragraphs.title: Marital Faithfulness and Rejection of Adultery

easy.explanation: Job speaks of his heart being deceived by a woman.
easy.q: By what did Job deny being enticed?

easy.explanation: He says, “if I have laid wait at my neighbour’s door.”
easy.q: At whose door did Job deny lying in wait?

easy.explanation: The passage calls it an heinous crime and an iniquity.
easy.q: How is adultery described?

medium.explanation: The sin is compared to a fire that consumes and roots out increase.
medium.q: What might happen to a person who commits the sin described here?

medium.explanation: The phrase emphasizes the grave nature of adultery.
medium.q: What does “heinous crime” communicate in this context?

answers: The hidden act is shown as destructive
They describe two kinds of wealth
medium.explanation: The door suggests secret temptation, while the fire suggests ruinous results.
medium.q: How are the waiting at the door and the fire related?

answers: To emphasize harm to the marriage bond
challenge.explanation: The wording highlights the violation of another man’s marriage.
challenge.q: Why does Job mention both the woman and her husband?

challenge.explanation: Fire represents a destructive consequence.
challenge.q: What does the image of fire add to the description of adultery?

answers: Faithfulness is a personal and social duty
challenge.explanation: Job rejects both the temptation and the betrayal involved.
challenge.q: What moral position emerges from the passage?

easy.explanation: He refers to the cause of his manservant and maidservant.
easy.q: Whose cause did Job say he did not despise?

easy.explanation: Job asks whether the same God made both of them.
easy.q: Who made both Job and his servant?

easy.explanation: The verse speaks of being made in the womb.
easy.q: Where were Job and his servant formed?

answers: They were made by the same God
medium.explanation: Shared creation grounds his argument for dignity and justice.
medium.q: What is Job’s reason for treating servants fairly?

answers: A claim or matter to be heard
medium.explanation: Job refers to the servant’s case or grievance.
medium.q: What does “cause” mean in “the cause of my manservant”?

answers: It stresses a common human origin
medium.explanation: Both master and servant share the same created human beginning.
medium.q: How does the reference to the womb support Job’s moral point?

challenge.explanation: Job recognizes that servants’ claims must be heard.
challenge.q: What view of authority appears in Job’s words?

challenge.explanation: The same Creator gives a basis for equal respect.
challenge.q: Why is God’s creation especially important in this discussion?

challenge.explanation: The two terms reinforce the fact that God formed them both.
challenge.q: What is the connection between “made” and “fashioned”?

paragraphs.title: Care for the Poor, Widows, Orphans, and the Unclothed

easy.explanation: He mentions the poor and the widow.
easy.q: Whom did Job say he had helped?

easy.explanation: Job says the fatherless ate with him.
easy.q: Who did not eat Job’s morsel alone?

easy.explanation: He describes warming the person with his sheep’s fleece.
easy.q: What did Job give to one without clothing?

answers: Lifting up his hand against him
medium.explanation: Job denies lifting his hand against the fatherless.
medium.q: What action toward the fatherless did Job deny?

medium.explanation: Job says he did not withhold what the poor needed.
medium.q: What does “their desire” refer to in relation to the poor?

answers: Both are basic needs he did not withhold
Both are merely signs of wealth
medium.explanation: He gives food to the fatherless and covering to the poor.
medium.q: How are food and clothing related in Job’s actions?

answers: He used public power against him
He did not use his position to harm him
challenge.explanation: The gate was a place of public authority and judgment.
challenge.q: What does the mention of the gate suggest about Job’s treatment of the fatherless?

challenge.explanation: Job describes meeting several basic needs of vulnerable people.
challenge.q: What principle connects the poor, widow, fatherless, and unclothed?

answers: Abusing the powerless is a serious sin
challenge.explanation: Job says fear of God restrained him from such abuse.
challenge.q: Why would Job accept punishment if he harmed the fatherless?

paragraphs.title: Independence from Wealth and Rejection of Idolatry

easy.explanation: He says he did not make gold his hope or confidence.
easy.q: In what did Job deny placing his hope?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions the sun and moon.
easy.q: What heavenly bodies does Job mention?

easy.explanation: He says his mouth had not kissed his hand in worship.
easy.q: What idolatrous gesture did Job reject?

answers: Both can become substitutes for trust in God
medium.explanation: Job rejects trusting in wealth and worshiping heavenly bodies.
medium.q: What connection does the passage make between wealth and idolatry?

medium.explanation: Job denies making fine gold his source of security.
medium.q: What does “my confidence” mean in “Thou art my confidence”?

answers: It would deny the God above
medium.explanation: Job says such worship would deny God.
medium.q: Why would worshiping the sun or moon be an iniquity?

answers: Job refuses to make them his security or object of worship
They are gifts for the poor
challenge.explanation: Job rejects both material trust and heavenly worship.
challenge.q: What do gold, wealth, the sun, and the moon have in common here?

answers: The passage joins inward attraction with outward worship
challenge.explanation: The heart is enticed and the mouth kisses the hand.
challenge.q: Why does Job mention both his heart and his mouth?

answers: Loyalty to God rather than wealth or heavenly bodies
Loyalty to the king rather than the poor
Loyalty to wealth rather than justice
challenge.explanation: Job refuses to replace God with riches or created things.
challenge.q: What central loyalty is expressed in this passage?

paragraphs.title: Restraint Toward Enemies and Generous Hospitality

easy.explanation: Job says he did not rejoice at the destruction of one who hated him.
easy.q: At what did Job say he did not rejoice?

easy.explanation: He did not let his mouth sin by cursing his enemy.
easy.q: What did Job not allow his mouth to do?

easy.explanation: He says he opened his doors to the traveller.
easy.q: To whom did Job open his doors?

answers: He refrains from rejoicing over the enemy and welcomes the stranger
He rejoices over the enemy and rejects the stranger
medium.explanation: The passage combines restraint toward enemies with hospitality.
medium.q: What contrast appears between Job’s enemy and the stranger?

medium.explanation: Job refuses to celebrate his enemy’s calamity.
medium.q: What does “destruction” mean in “the destruction of him that hated me”?

answers: Both prevent adding evil to the enemy’s trouble
medium.explanation: Job does not celebrate the trouble or wish further harm.

answers: An enemy outside versus a traveller welcomed inside
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from an enemy’s destruction to an open door for a stranger.

answers: He does not desire his enemy’s death
He refuses to feed an orphan
challenge.explanation: He will not let his mouth curse the enemy’s soul.
challenge.q: What does Job’s refusal to wish a curse show?

challenge.explanation: Job controls hostility and practices open hospitality.
challenge.q: What quality joins both parts of the passage?

paragraphs.title: Open Confession and Freedom from Public Fear

easy.explanation: He denies covering his transgressions or hiding his iniquity.
easy.q: What did Job deny hiding?

answers: A great multitude and family contempt

easy.q: What did Job say did not terrify him?

easy.explanation: He presents himself as willing to speak openly.
easy.q: What would Job do if he had committed sins?

answers: To show that silence was not concealment of guilt
medium.explanation: He rejects fear of public opinion as the reason for silence.
medium.q: Why does Job say he did not keep silence from fear?

medium.explanation: The image describes keeping wrongdoing hidden.
medium.q: What does “hiding mine iniquity in my bosom” mean?

answers: Both could suggest concealment or fear

A man determined to hide everything

answers: Job presents himself as ready to hear every charge
challenge.explanation: His openness leads to his request for a written accusation.

easy.explanation: He wishes that his adversary had written a book.
easy.q: What did Job want to receive?

answers: On his shoulder like a crown

answers: So he could answer each charge

answers: The rows or lines made by plowing

A desire to conceal the charges
